At the door, in Prenzlauer Berg
Mara, a nurse from Sibiu, has just arrived in Berlin, where she got a job at a hospital. Her flat is in the Prenzlauer Berg district. She rings the landlord's doorbell to pick up the keys.
Good evening! Excuse me, are you Mr Brandt?
My name is Mara Ionescu. I'm the new tenant.
Ah, Ms Ionescu! Nice to meet you. You're not German, are you?
No, I'm not German. I'm Romanian.
I'm from Sibiu. In German the city is called Hermannstadt.
Hermannstadt! Lovely! I'm from Berlin, from right here. Are you a student?
No, I'm a nurse. I work at the hospital.
Very good! Welcome to Berlin! Here are the keys.
Thank you very much, Mr Brandt!
You're welcome. And this is Fritz, my dachshund. Good night, Ms Ionescu! See you tomorrow!

Say “e” (as in “bed”) with your lips rounded as if for “o”.
“ß” (Eszett) is read as a long, clear “s”: “heiße” = “HIGH-seh”.
“ei” is read “eye” (mein = “mine”), while “ie” is read as a long “ee” (Sie = “zee”). Easy to mix up!
S before a vowel is pronounced “z”: Sie = “zee”, sehr = “zair”. “sch” = “sh”: schön = “shön”.
Germans greet each other often and fairly formally. Your choice depends on the time of day and on how well you know the person.
In southern Germany and in Austria you'll hear “Grüß Gott” (hello / good day) and “Servus” (hi). In Berlin, “Guten Tag” and “Hallo” are the most common.
Unlike English, German has a polite form of “you”: “Sie” (formal you), ALWAYS written with a capital letter. “Du” (informal you) is used with friends, family, children and young colleagues.
a stranger, an adult, a boss
a friend, a child, a young colleague
Germans use “Sie” a lot, much more than you might expect. When someone suggests “Wir können uns duzen” (we can say “du” to each other), it's a sign of friendship.
“Sie” with a capital letter = you (formal). “sie” with a small letter = she or they. The context and the capital letter make the difference.
As in English, the pronoun is NOT left out: “I am Mara” = “Ich bin Mara”, not “Bin Mara”.
Good news: in German, the profession is said without an article: “Ich bin Krankenschwester” = “I'm a nurse” (literally “I am nurse”). (English is different here: you need “a”.)
The feminine form is usually made with -in: Student → Studentin, Lehrer → Lehrerin.
5. Nouns: always with a capital letter
In German, ALL nouns are written with a capital letter, wherever they are in the sentence: das Krankenhaus, die Stadt, der Schlüssel, der Dackel.
The negation “nicht” usually comes after the verb (like “not” in English).
In “yes / no” questions, the verb moves to FIRST place:
“…, oder?” at the end = “…, isn't it? / right?”: “Sie sind nicht Deutsche, oder?”
